content: Innovative performance can be enhanced through two primary mechanisms: acquiring knowledge from external sources and utilizing external pathways to commercialize knowledge resources that have been developed internally. Within organizations, various factors influence the sharing of knowledge. These include internal adoption and adaptation processes, as well as external inputs such as published research, regional and national meetings, professional societies, and collaborations with external colleagues. These elements are particularly important when developing new ideas. Greenhalgh has outlined a spectrum of management roles in the diffusion of innovation, which include: Allowing innovation to emerge naturally, as described in complexity science (Let it happen). Facilitating the process of innovation (Help it happen). Actively driving and implementing innovation (Make it happen). Rigid hierarchical structures within organizations can hinder the sharing of knowledge. Interestingly, workplace stress, while often seen as detrimental, can paradoxically enhance innovation and creativity. Recommendations to promote knowledge sharing are available and should be implemented to foster a more collaborative environment. A growth mindset, both among employees and within management, is a critical factor in fostering innovation. Regarding employee characteristics, the process of idea elaboration benefits from a strategic approach known as inside-out network sequencing. This involves mobilizing input and support from close, inner-circle connections before reaching out to more distant, outer-circle networks. This approach has been shown to provide a performance advantage in innovation. Conscientiousness, defined as the tendency to plan and coordinate effectively with others, has been found to amplify the effectiveness of proactive behaviors within teams and organizations. Leadership approaches also play a pivotal role in fostering innovation. These include: Complexity leadership, which focuses on enabling adaptive and emergent processes. Humble leadership, characterized by openness, self-awareness, and a willingness to learn from others. Hubristic leadership, which, in contrast, may hinder innovation due to overconfidence and a lack of receptiveness to new ideas. Barriers to innovation include phenomena such as the not invented here syndrome, where organizations resist adopting external ideas or solutions, thereby stifling potential progress.
